history.summary: The Leaning Temple of Huma at Huma village, ~23 km south of Sambalpur on the left bank of the Mahanadi (CSV town 'Sambalpur' corrected to Huma), is one of the very few leaning temples in the world. Legend says worship began when a milkman (Gauda) found a rock on the riverbank drinking up his daily milk offering; a cowherd likewise saw his cow pouring milk on the spot, revealing the Sivalinga. Historical accounts credit the original temple to the Ganga emperor Anangabhima Deva III, with rebuilding/renovation by Chauhan King Baliar Singh (1660-1690) and further works under King Ajit Singh (1766-1788). The main shrine leans ~13.8 degrees to the north-east while its pinnacle stays perpendicular; whether by design or from displacement of the rocky riverbed (floods/earthquakes) is UNRESOLVED. It is an ASI-protected monument. The stretch of Mahanadi behind the temple hosts the sacred 'Kudo' fish, considered the deity's own and never caught; devotees feed them. Architecture: rekha vimana, flat-roofed jagamohana, pillared Nandi mandapa, Pancharatha plan.

name: Leaning Temple of Huma (Bimaleswar Temple)
town_description: Huma is a riverside village in Sambalpur district, Odisha, situated on the left bank of the Mahanadi about 23 km south of Sambalpur city. It is a small pilgrimage settlement built around the leaning Bimaleswar temple and its ghats, where devotees feed the sacred Kudo fish in the river. The area is agricultural, typical of the Mahanadi valley in western Odisha.
